approachQuestion.prompt:
Compare Fragmented Messages

Two arrays left and right contain fragments of lowercase ASCII text. Return true exactly when concatenating left in array order would produce the same text as concatenating right. Empty fragments are legal, and fragment boundaries have no meaning in the result.

Example 1: left = ["ab","","c"], right = ["a","bc"] → true.
Example 2: left = ["ab","c"], right = ["ab","d"] → false.
Example 3: left = [], right = ["",""] → true.
Example 4: left = ["a"], right = ["a","b"] → false.

Constraints:
0 ≤ left.length, right.length ≤ 200,000.
Each fragment contains only a–z and may be empty; each side contains at most 200,000 characters in total.
Do not modify either array or any fragment. Return one Boolean.
constraints: Each fragment contains only a–z and may be empty; each side contains at most 200,000 characters in total.
Do not modify either array or any fragment. Return one Boolean.

options.text: Maintain a fragment index and character offset for each side. Skip exhausted or empty fragments, compare the next characters, and advance. Accept only if both sides run out together without a mismatch.
options.feedback: The cursors compare the logical text in order without requiring the fragment boundaries to match. Joint exhaustion checks for a leftover suffix.

options.text: Join all fragments on each side into a separate flat string, then compare the two strings.
options.feedback: This is correct for the entire domain, including empty fragments. The two flat copies consume removable temporary storage; cursors can read the original fragments.

options.text: Require equal array lengths, then compare fragments at corresponding array indices for exact equality.
options.feedback: Boundaries can differ even when the messages agree. ["ab","c"] and ["a","bc"] both represent "abc" but this method rejects them.

options.text: Walk the logical characters on both sides until either side ends. Return true if all characters compared so far match.
options.feedback: A common prefix is insufficient. For ["a"] and ["a","b"], this returns true although one side has an extra character.

feedback.reason: Physical fragments do not define logical message boundaries.
details: Keep a fragment index and character offset per side. Skip exhausted fragments, compare available characters, and advance the offsets. On exhaustion, accept only when neither side has a character remaining.

Physical fragments do not define logical message boundaries. Skip empty fragments and exhausted offsets before comparing the next characters. Equal prefixes are insufficient when one side still has a suffix; success requires both logical sequences to end together.

“Maintain a fragment index and character offset for each side. Skip exhausted or empty fragments, compare the next characters, and advance. Accept only if both sides run out together without a mismatch.”: The cursors compare the logical text in order without requiring the fragment boundaries to match. Joint exhaustion checks for a leftover suffix.

“Join all fragments on each side into a separate flat string, then compare the two strings.”: This is correct for the entire domain, including empty fragments. The two flat copies consume removable temporary storage; cursors can read the original fragments.

“Require equal array lengths, then compare fragments at corresponding array indices for exact equality.”: Boundaries can differ even when the messages agree. ["ab","c"] and ["a","bc"] both represent "abc" but this method rejects them.

“Walk the logical characters on both sides until either side ends. Return true if all characters compared so far match.”: A common prefix is insufficient. For ["a"] and ["a","b"], this returns true although one side has an extra character.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Cursors Across Fragments”, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let F be the total number of fragments across both arrays and C the total number of characters across both arrays. State a bound tight as a function of these input sizes over all legal inputs, including empty arrays. Character access, length reads and index updates cost constant time. No substring copies, recursion or hashing are used. Exclude the input and Boolean output; include all cursor and call-stack space.
constraints: Each fragment contains only a–z and may be empty; each side contains at most 200,000 characters in total.
Do not modify either array or any fragment. Return one Boolean.

options.text: O(F + C + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space.
O(F + C + 1) time, O(C + 1) auxiliary space.
O((F + C + 1)²) time, O(1) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Account for both fragment headers and compared characters, including empty fragments.
details: Each visited fragment is skipped once and each compared character is read once. In the worst case the messages agree through their ends, so the scan traverses the relevant input sizes. Empty fragments still cost work; the +1 covers both arrays being empty. Only four cursors and fixed control state are stored.
The option “O(F + C + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: Both fragments and characters can contribute work, with only fixed cursor storage.
The option “O(C + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: This omits traversal of arbitrarily many empty fragments when C=0.
The option “O(F + C + 1) time, O(C + 1) auxiliary space.”: This counts flat string copies that the cursor method never creates.
The option “O((F + C + 1)²) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: The fragment and offset indices advance; no prefix is repeatedly scanned.
